findings.title: The self-check "none" marker is a regex, but wrong_reason matches markers as substrings and needs an error list
quotes: has the none marker regex `^ran 0 tests`
if (name == "pytest" and code == 5) or any(m in output for m in r["none"]):
marker = next((m for m in r["error"] if m in output)
findings.fix: give the entry `"error": []` and the substring marker `"ran 0 tests"`, as the other runners do. If an anchored match is really wanted, say that CT-3 changes `wrong_reason` to use regexes, and for which runners.

sources.situation: every existing `RUNNERS` entry lists plain substrings under `none` and `error`, and `wrong_reason` tests them with `m in output`. The literal `^ran 0 tests` never appears in any output, so this path never refuses with "no tests ran". CT-3 also gives the entry no `error` key, so `r["error"]` raises KeyError the first time red, `suite()` or evidence's `crashed` reads a self-check run.

`wrong_reason` tests each marker with `m in output`, so the literal text `^ran 0 tests` never occurs and a regex marker never matches. FR-4's refusal "whatever the exit code" would not fire if the contract is built as written. `wrong_reason` also reads `r["error"]` unconditionally, and CT-3 gives self-check no `error` key, so the call raises KeyError. CT-4's `collect` calls `wrong_reason(name, ...)` with this same name. Separately, FR-4 says the output "ends its run with" `ran 0 tests`, but `^ran 0 tests` can match anywhere in the output. In a multi-file suite, one file that prints `ran 0 tests, 0 failed` makes `crashed` true in `collect`. Every test then reads "didn't run", including those of passing files that printed `ok`. That contradicts AC-9 and FR-8.

findings.reason: CT-3 gives `RUNNERS["self-check"]` the none marker "regex `^ran 0 tests`", but `wrong_reason` (implement.py:58-61) tests `m in output` over plain strings and reads `r["error"]` unconditionally. Built as written, the marker never matches, and the missing `error` key raises KeyError.
findings.note: CT-7 gives self-check plain substring markers and an empty error list, read by wrong_reason unchanged

findings.title: A readable self-check suite lets a crashed file pass the epic-closing review
quotes: `suite()` sums every count line's number (the suite prints one per file), so `collected` is the suite's total
elif r["runner"] is None or r["failing"] is None:
if not quick and r["collected"] is not None and base.get("collected") is not None and r["collected"] < base["collected"]:
findings.fix: add a rule to CT-3 that a self-check suite exiting non-zero with no `FAIL` line fails review (or counts as broken), and add a test for it beside TC-6.

sources.situation: today a self-check suite has no known runner, so `review()` fails any non-zero suite ("its runner is unknown"). Under CT-3 the runner becomes `self-check` and `failing` becomes a list. Take a file that crashes at import: it prints no `FAIL` line, the runner has no error markers so the suite isn't `broken`, and `failing` is `[]`. With `tests.epic` set (`quick`), the collected-count check is skipped too. The review then passes on a suite that exited non-zero. CT-3 never says what review does with a non-zero self-check suite that has no `FAIL` line.

the task closing an epic runs `review()`, which runs `suite()`. A suite where file A crashes before its `ran` line and files B and C print theirs makes the runner "self-check", not None. `failing` is `[]` because there is no FAIL line, and the exit code is 1. `review()` adds the reason "the suite exits N and its runner is unknown" only for `r["runner"] is None or r["failing"] is None`. `broken` is false, because `wrong_reason` finds no marker. So `new = []`, no reason is recorded, and the review passes a suite that exits non-zero. Before this change, that suite's runner was unknown and the review refused it. CT-4 closes this hole for evidence only (`failed` when the suite exits non-zero), and CT-3 says nothing about review.

findings.reason: implement.py:578-580 records "exits N and its runner is unknown" only when `runner is None or failing is None`. Under CT-3 a crashed self-check file leaves runner "self-check" and `failing` `[]`, with no error markers, so `new` is empty. The review passes a suite that exited non-zero, and CT-3 and CT-4 say nothing about review.
findings.note: CT-3: review fails a non-zero self-check suite with no FAIL line; TC-12 added

findings.title: US-3 is said to need only Foundation, but CT-4 needs what CT-3 delivers

the runner is `implement.runner(suite command, suite output)`
findings.fix: make US-3 depend on US-1, or move the `runner`/`RUNNERS`/`SUMMARY` part of CT-3 into Foundation.

sources.situation: CT-4 calls the two-argument `runner` and reads `SUMMARY["self-check"]`. CT-3 defines both, and CT-3 is delivered by the US-1 block. Today `runner(command)` takes one argument and `SUMMARY` has no self-check entry. If US-3 is built beside US-1 or first, `collect` has nothing to call. The Foundation block (CT-1, CT-2) only makes the scripts print lines, so a sequential run of US-3 right after Foundation fails.

findings.reason: plan.md says US-3 depends only on Foundation, but CT-4 calls the two-argument `implement.runner` and reads `SUMMARY["self-check"]`. Both come from CT-3, which is delivered by US-1, so US-3 built before or beside US-1 has nothing to call.
findings.note: runner/RUNNERS/SUMMARY moved to CT-7, delivered by Foundation

findings.title: TC-9 can't catch a FAIL line matched by test name alone
quotes: `tests/test_b.py` `test_one` is `passed` (same name as a test in the failing file)
A failing-test entry of the form `<file>::<name>` matches a test only when both its file and its name match
else "failed" if any(re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(short)}\b", x) for x in failing)
findings.fix: make the failing test share its name with the other file's passing test. For example, `test_a.py` prints `FAIL tests/test_a.py::test_one`, and the assert says `tests/test_b.py` `test_one` is `passed`.

sources.situation: the only `FAIL` line in the fixture is `tests/test_a.py::test_two`, and no other file has a `test_two`. If evidence keeps today's name-only regex for `FAIL` entries, the test still passes. Yet a real `FAIL tests/test_a.py::test_one` would mark `tests/test_b.py` `test_one` as `failed`, which breaks AC-9's "no test of another file is `failed`".

findings.reason: TC-9's only `FAIL` line is `test_a.py::test_two`, and no other file has a `test_two`. So today's name-only regex (evidence.py:436) would also pass the test. The comment "same name as a test in the failing file" is wrong, because `test_a.py::test_one` is the passing one, not the failing one.
findings.note: TC-9: the failing test shares its name with the other file's passing test

findings.title: No test proves the self-check scripts run through `selfcheck.main` (CT-2)
quotes: the same change in every `tests/test_*.py` `__main__` block
- Covers: CT-1
findings.fix: add a test that reads every `tests/test_*.py` and checks its `__main__` block ends in a `selfcheck.main(...)` call. Or run each script with one test name and check it prints `ran 1 tests`.

sources.situation: TC-1, TC-2, TC-3 and TC-11 run only a generated `tests/test_demo.py`. A script left with today's `for name, test in list(globals().items())` loop, or with its fixed list in the wrong order, passes every planned test. Yet `python tests/<that file> test_new` still runs the whole file and prints no `ran` line, so red reads it as an unknown runner and accepts it as today. Evidence also gets no per-test lines for that file.

findings.reason: TC-1, TC-2, TC-3 and TC-11 run only the generated `tests/test_demo.py`, and tests.md has no test over the real `tests/test_*.py` `__main__` blocks. A script left with the old `globals()` loop would pass every planned test.
findings.note: TC-13 checks every script's __main__ calls selfcheck.main

findings.title: TC-9 and TC-10 fixtures may lack the `def` lines their expected results need
quotes: `test_a.py` prints `ok tests/test_a.py::test_one`, `FAIL tests/test_a.py::test_two`, `ran 2 tests, 1 failed` and exits 1

sources.situation: `collect` reads each test's line with `asserts_in`, and a test with no `def` gets `didn't run`. A fixture that only prints those lines yields `didn't run` for tests the assert expects as `passed` or `failed`. The writer may then fit the code to the fixture, not to CT-4.
